questions.q: **FLOW : UOLD :: GRIP : ?**
questions.solution: Each letter of FLOW is replaced by its **opposite letter** (the pair adds up to 27): F(6) and U(21), L(12) and O(15), O(15) and L(12), W(23) and D(4). Opposites of GRIP: G(7) to T(20), R(18) to I(9), I(9) to R(18), P(16) to K(11) — **TIRK**.
questions.shortcut: Spot opposite pairs with the 27-sum rule (or the EJOTY / AZ-BY-CX memory list).
Both second numbers sit just below a cube: n³ − 1.

questions.q: **Thermometer : Temperature :: Anemometer : ?**
questions.solution: A thermometer measures temperature; an anemometer measures **wind speed**. The other options belong to other instruments: humidity (hygrometer), air pressure (barometer), rainfall (rain gauge).
questions.shortcut: Instrument : what it measures.

questions.q: Find the odd number pair: **6 – 35, 8 – 63, 10 – 99, 12 – 145**
questions.solution: In each pair the second number is (first)² − 1: 6² − 1 = 35, 8² − 1 = 63, 10² − 1 = 99. But 12² − 1 = 143, not 145, so **12 – 145** is the odd pair.

questions.q: Find the odd one out: **Tabla, Mridangam, Sitar, Dholak**
questions.solution: Tabla, Mridangam and Dholak are **percussion** instruments (played by striking a drum skin). The **Sitar** is a string instrument, so it is the odd one.
questions.shortcut: Group by how the instrument is played: struck vs plucked.

questions.q: Find the next term: **4, 9, 25, 49, 121, ?**
questions.solution: The terms are squares of consecutive **prime numbers**: 2², 3², 5², 7², 11². The next prime after 11 is 13, so the next term is 13² = **169**. (144 = 12² is the trap — 12 is not prime.)
questions.shortcut: Take square roots: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 are primes, so next is 13².

questions.q: Find the next letter: **C, F, J, O, U, ?**
questions.solution: Positions: C = 3, F = 6, J = 10, O = 15, U = 21. The gaps grow: +3, +4, +5, +6, so the next gap is +7. 21 + 7 = 28, and after Z the count restarts: 28 − 26 = 2 = **B**.
questions.shortcut: Growing gap; when you cross Z, subtract 26.
questions.pattern: letter series (growing gap, wrap past Z)

questions.q: Find the next term: **BF2, DH6, FJ12, HL20, ?**
questions.solution: Both letters move +2 each time: B, D, F, H, **J** and F, H, J, L, **N**. The numbers are 1 × 2, 2 × 3, 3 × 4, 4 × 5, so next is 5 × 6 = **30**. Next term: **JN30**.
questions.shortcut: Split into letter part (+2, +2) and number part n(n + 1).

questions.q: In a certain code language, **PLANET** is written as **UFOBMQ**. How will **GARDEN** be written in that language?
questions.solution: Write PLANET in reverse: TENALP. Now move every letter +1: T to U, E to F, N to O, A to B, L to M, P to Q — **UFOBMQ**. For GARDEN: reverse gives NEDRAG, then +1 gives **OFESBH**.
questions.shortcut: If the code's first letter is near the word's last letter, suspect 'reverse, then shift'.

questions.q: If **ROSE** is coded as **6821** and **CHAIR** is coded as **73456**, how will **SEARCH** be coded?
questions.solution: Match letters to digits position by position. ROSE = 6821 gives R = 6, O = 8, S = 2, E = 1. CHAIR = 73456 gives C = 7, H = 3, A = 4, I = 5, R = 6 (R = 6 again, confirming the code). SEARCH = S E A R C H = 2 1 4 6 7 3 = **214673**.
questions.shortcut: Build a letter-digit table once, then read the new word off it.

questions.q:
If **A** means **÷**, **B** means **×**, **C** means **+** and **D** means **−**, find the value of

**36 A 4 B 5 C 12 D 7**
questions.solution: Replace the letters: 36 ÷ 4 × 5 + 12 − 7. BODMAS, ÷ and × left to right: 36 ÷ 4 = 9, 9 × 5 = 45. Then 45 + 12 − 7 = **50**. (Swapping C and D by mistake gives 40.)
questions.shortcut: Rewrite with signs, then BODMAS.

questions.solution: Row rule: (first)² + (second)². Check: 5² + 3² = 25 + 9 = 34 and 6² + 2² = 36 + 4 = 40. So 7² + 4² = 49 + 16 = **65**.
questions.shortcut: Third number far bigger than the product: try sum of squares.

questions.q:
**A # B** means A is the father of B, **A $ B** means A is the brother of B, and **A @ B** means A is the wife of B.

If **P # Q $ R @ S**, how is **P** related to **S**?
questions.solution: Decode left to right: P # Q — P is the father of Q. Q $ R — Q is the brother of R, so R is also P's child. R @ S — R is the wife of S, so R is P's daughter and S is her husband. P is the father of S's wife, i.e. P is S's **father-in-law**.
questions.shortcut: Chain the symbols one link at a time; a daughter's husband makes the father a father-in-law.

questions.q: **Arjun** is the only brother of **Kavya's** mother. How is Arjun's father related to Kavya?
questions.solution: Arjun and Kavya's mother are siblings, so Arjun's father is also the father of Kavya's mother. The mother's father is Kavya's (maternal) **grandfather**.
questions.shortcut: Mother's brother's father = mother's father.

questions.q: Starting from his house, **Neeraj** walks 10 m towards south, turns left and walks 6 m, turns left again and walks 18 m, and then turns right and walks 9 m. How far and in which direction is he now from his house?
questions.solution: Take the house as (0, 0). South 10 m: (0, −10). Facing south, a left turn faces **east**: 6 m gives (6, −10). Another left faces **north**: 18 m gives (6, 8). A right turn faces **east**: 9 m gives (15, 8). Distance = √(15² + 8²) = √289 = **17 m**; he is east and north of the house, so **North-East**.
questions.shortcut: Net east 6 + 9 = 15, net north 18 − 10 = 8; (8, 15, 17) is a Pythagorean triplet.

questions.q: In a row of students, **Priya** is 14th from the left end and **Rohit** is 17th from the right end. When they interchange their positions, Priya becomes **22nd from the left** end. How many students are there in the row?
questions.solution: After the interchange Priya stands exactly where Rohit stood. So Rohit's old place is 22nd from the left and 17th from the right. Total = 22 + 17 − 1 = **38**. (Adding 14 + 17 = 31 uses the wrong pair of positions.)
questions.shortcut: Same seat seen from both ends: left + right − 1.

questions.q: Six friends **A, B, C, D, E and F** sit around a circular table, equally spaced and facing the centre. **A** sits opposite **D**. **F** sits second to the left of **D**. **B** is not an immediate neighbour of **A**. **C** sits to the immediate right of **E**. Who sits opposite **C**?
questions.solution: Number the seats 1 to 6 clockwise with A at seat 1; for people facing the centre, **left = clockwise**. D is opposite A: seat 4. F is second to the left of D: seat 6. A's neighbours are seats 2 and 6, so B (not next to A) must take seat 3 or 5. C is immediately right of E, i.e. C is one seat anticlockwise of E. With seats 2, 3, 5 free, the only fit is E = 3, C = 2, which leaves B = 5. Clockwise order: A, C, E, D, B, F. Opposite C (seat 2) is seat 5: **B**.
questions.shortcut: Fix A, place the opposite/definite clues first, then test the pair clue in the remaining seats.

questions.q:
**Statements:** Some doctors are teachers. All teachers are singers.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some doctors are singers.
II. All singers are doctors.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
questions.solution: The doctors who are teachers lie inside Singers (all teachers are singers), so some doctors are definitely singers — I **follows**. Singers can include many people who are neither teachers nor doctors, so II **does not follow**. Answer: **Only I**.
questions.shortcut: Some + All (in that order) gives a 'Some' conclusion; 'All' reversed never follows.

questions.q: In the given diagram, the circles represent **Players**, **Singers** and **Graduates**, and the numbers show how many persons are in each region. How many **graduates are either players or singers, but not both**?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 170 150" width="170" height="150" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="62" cy="58" r="40"/><circle cx="108" cy="58" r="40"/><circle cx="85" cy="98" r="40"/><text x="42" y="52" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">12</text><text x="128" y="52" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">9</text><text x="85" y="126" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">15</text><text x="85" y="44" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">5</text><text x="57" y="92" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">7</text><text x="113" y="92" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">4</text><text x="85" y="76" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">3</text><text x="18" y="16" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">Players</text><text x="152" y="16" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">Singers</text><text x="85" y="146" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">Graduates</text></svg>
questions.solution: We need the Graduates circle, but only the parts shared with exactly one of the other two circles: Graduates ∩ Players only = 7, and Graduates ∩ Singers only = 4. The centre (3) is excluded because those persons are both players and singers. Answer = 7 + 4 = **11**.
questions.shortcut: Pick the two lens regions inside Graduates, leave out the centre.

questions.q:
Arrange the following words in the order in which they would appear in an English dictionary.

1. Sequence  2. Sequential  3. Sequel  4. Sequin  5. Sequester
questions.solution: All five begin with **sequ**. The 5th letter splits them: Sequ**e**l, Sequ**e**nce, Sequ**e**ntial, Sequ**e**ster come before Sequ**i**n. Among the 'seque-' words compare the 6th letter: seque**l** (l) < seque**n**ce, seque**n**tial (n) < seque**s**ter (s). Sequence is a prefix of Sequential, so it comes first. Order: Sequel (3), Sequence (1), Sequential (2), Sequester (5), Sequin (4) — **3, 1, 2, 5, 4**.
questions.shortcut: A word that is the start of another word always comes before it.

questions.q:
**Statement:** Most of the students who scored above 90% in the board examination had taken coaching at Sunrise Academy.

**Conclusions:**
I. Every student who takes coaching at Sunrise Academy scores above 90%.
II. A student who does not take coaching cannot score above 90%.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
questions.solution: The statement is about **toppers**: most of them went to the academy. I reverses this into a claim about **every** academy student — the statement says nothing of academy students who scored less, so I does not follow. II is an extreme claim; 'most' toppers means some toppers did not take this coaching, and nothing is said about uncoached students at all. Neither follows.
questions.shortcut: Watch for reversed direction (A mostly B does not mean B always A) and 'cannot/every' words.

questions.q: How many triangles are there in the given figure?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 154 118" width="154" height="118" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="77" y1="5" x2="5" y2="113"/><line x1="5" y1="113" x2="149" y2="113"/><line x1="149" y1="113" x2="77" y2="5"/><line x1="41" y1="59" x2="113" y2="59"/><line x1="113" y1="59" x2="77" y2="113"/><line x1="77" y1="113" x2="41" y2="59"/><line x1="77" y1="5" x2="77" y2="113"/></svg>
questions.solution:
The inner triangle joins the mid-points of the sides, and a vertical line runs from the top vertex to the middle of the base. Count by size:

- **Smallest pieces:** the top triangle is cut into 2 halves, the inverted centre triangle is cut into 2 halves, plus the 2 bottom-corner triangles — 6.
- **Whole top triangle** and **whole inverted triangle** — 2.
- **Top half + centre half on each side** (apex, side mid-point, base mid-point) — 2.
- **Each half of the big triangle** (split by the vertical line) — 2.
- **The big triangle** — 1.

Total = 6 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = **13**.
questions.shortcut: Count in size layers and note each layer's left/right symmetry to avoid double counting.

questions.solution: A vertical mirror on the right reverses the order of the characters (the last one, 2, comes first) and flips each character left-to-right. None of B, J, 5, K, F, 2 is left-right symmetric, so every character appears reversed. Only the option that both reverses the order and flips every character is correct.
questions.shortcut: Mirror on the side: order reverses and each character flips sideways; top and bottom stay.

questions.q: A square sheet of paper is folded as shown by the dashed lines and arrows, and then punched at the marked position(s). How will the sheet look when it is completely unfolded?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 60 60" width="60" height="60" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="6,6 54,6 54,54 6,54"/><circle cx="12" cy="24" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="12" cy="36" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="48" cy="24" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="48" cy="36" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 60 60" width="60" height="60" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="6,6 54,6 54,54 6,54"/><circle cx="48" cy="24" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="48" cy="36" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.solution: The left half is folded onto the right half, then the top half is folded down; the punch, near the right edge just below the horizontal crease, goes through all four layers. Unfold the second fold: the hole is reflected across the horizontal centre line, giving a second hole near the right edge just above the centre line. Unfold the first fold: both are reflected across the vertical centre line to the left edge. Result: **4 holes** — a close pair near the middle of the right edge and a close pair near the middle of the left edge, each pair straddling the horizontal centre line.
questions.shortcut: Unfold in reverse order; each fold doubles the holes as mirror images across that crease.

questions.q: The given sheet is folded to form a cube. Which face will be opposite to the face showing **R**? (Ignore the orientation of the letters/numbers.)
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 102 78" width="102" height="78" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="27,3 51,3 51,27 27,27"/><text x="39" y="20" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">P</text><polygon points="3,27 27,27 27,51 3,51"/><text x="15" y="44" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">Q</text><polygon points="27,27 51,27 51,51 27,51"/><text x="39" y="44" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">R</text><polygon points="51,27 75,27 75,51 51,51"/><text x="63" y="44" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">S</text><polygon points="75,27 99,27 99,51 75,51"/><text x="87" y="44" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">T</text><polygon points="27,51 51,51 51,75 27,75"/><text x="39" y="68" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">U</text></svg>
questions.solution: In a straight strip of four faces (Q, R, S, T), alternate faces are opposite: Q–S and **R–T**. The two faces sticking out (P above R, U below R) are opposite each other. So the face opposite R is **T**.
questions.shortcut: Row of four: skip one face to find the opposite.
